speechtext: that Bill C-104, an Act to correct certain anomalies, inconsistencies, archaisms and errors and to deal with other matters of a non-controversial and uncomplicated nature in the Statutes of Canada be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there have been consultations involving the Parties. Certainly on behalf of the New Democratic Party, in view of the nature of this Bill we are prepared to see it go through all stages in the House today.
It is legislation that has already been reviewed by the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. It is an important and valuable process whereby legislation which has become in some way archaic or no longer in effect as a result of Government policy decisions can in fact be changed, whereby errors which have crept into legislation can be dealt with. Certainly we support the process.
The Bill in question has been dealt with. There were a couple of hearings by the committee on some of the more substantive provisions of the Bill. Given the unanimous support of the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, on behalf of the NDP. we are prepared to co-operate in the passage of this legislation in all stages through the House today.

speakeroldname: The Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speakerposition: Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
that Bill C-99, An Act to amend the Currency Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: The Bill before us is of a purely housekeeping nature. Its purpose is to ensure that the accounting procedures followed in determining the exchange fund's net income are consistent with those followed in the consolidated Public Accounts.

Hon. Members may recall that in 1985, the Auditor General of Canada recommended that several special government accounts, including that of the Exchange Fund, be consolidated in with the general government accounts. In his February, 1986 Budget the Minister of Finance announced revisions to the accounting policies of the Public Accounts of Canada in response to the Auditor General's recommendations. Among these were the consolidation of the Exchange Fund with the Consolidated Revenue Fund for purposes of determining the fiscal position of the Government.

The Exchange Fund is a special account of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) which serves as the principal repository of Canada's official international reserves. Although the Exchange Fund has been consolidated with the Consolidated Revenue Fund in the Public Accounts, it exists as a distinct accounting entity and is governed by separate legislation, namely, the Currency Act, which Bill C-99 proposes to amend.
The Currency Act contains a provision that differs from the accounting principles now followed in the Public Accounts. In determining that income the Currency Act calls for gains or losses from exchange rate changes, and these occur daily and weekly, and gold transactions to be averaged over three years, while such changes are recognized immediately in the Public Accounts. So there are two different accounting treatments.
The amendment we are proposing would repeal the three-year averaging provision in the Currency Act and require that the accounting principles applied to the Exchange Fund be consistent with those of the Public Accounts. This will remove an anomaly that was created by the consolidation introduced in 1986.
I would like to note that this amendment to the Currency Act has no financial implications and will not affect the actual operations of the Exchange Fund in any way. It is concerned only with the presentation of the Exchange Fund's financial statements, making them consistent with the presentation already contained in the Public Accounts and which is based on recommendations of the Auditor General. The Auditor General recommended this not just for the Exchange Fund but for other funds of the Government of Canada as well to bring them into consistency.
Finally, I would like to remark that the payment of income by the Exchange Fund to the Consolidated Revenue Fund is only a bookkeeping entry. No cash is transferred. Income from foreign currency assets is retained by the Exchange Fund and the Canadian dollar equivalent which is paid to the CRF is matched by an increase in Canadian dollar advances to the Exchange Fund from the CRF so that there is no change in cash holdings. The change also has no effect on the Government's deficit whose measurement is already determined by the accounting principles adopted last year.
I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that not only is this Bill of a housekeeping nature, and not only does it follow the recommendations of the Auditor General, but it makes overdue sense since the changes introduced in 1986, and I would urge the House to give it speedy consideration.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, as the Minister said, this Bill is a straightforward Bill which is changing certain methods of reporting and accounting in line with recommendations of the Auditor General. Therefore, it is the view of the Official Opposition that it is not a Bill which requires extensive debate or a Bill on which there would be controversy.
The original recommendation to change the methods of reflecting currency matters in the Public Accounts of Canada came from the Auditor General in 1980. Indeed, the audit report to the Minister of Finance for the year ended December 31, 1979, disclosed the matter of the Exchange Fund account as an item that should be brought to the attention of Parliament since it had not previously been disclosed in a manner which made it clear to Members of this House.
I want to put this in the context of the whole question of financial accountability. We in this House have all been pleased with the changes that were made in committees. There was all-Party support for many changes that were made in the way committees functioned. Indeed, we have seen some improvements with which we can all be very pleased. However, a weak link still exists in terms of financial accountability.
If we consider the original purpose for which Parliament was intended a few centuries ago we will see that it was originally intended to be a place where citizens could have their grievances redressed before they paid their taxes. Later on, at the time of American independence, there was the stirring statement "no taxation without representation". One of the basic functions of Parliament is to ensure that citizens have a voice in the way their taxes are spent and that there is proper accountability. In spite of the changes in the committee system with which we are all so pleased, a weak link still exists in financial accountability. I say this not in any partisan fashion because every Party in the House has to bear some responsibility for this.
When we have Estimates put before the House it is traditional under Vote 1, General Administration, that questions
January 22, 1988

can be asked about any aspect of that Department's administration and functions. What happens is that Members of the Opposition come in with whatever criticisms or complaints they have about the Department and they line up with them while the Government supporters line up to protect the Minister. Policy matters are discussed but it is very rare in the course of a debate on the Estimates to have a line-by-line examination of the costs.
Furthermore, since the rules were changed in the 1970s, an Estimates have gone out to different standing committees instead of being dealt with in the House. The advantage that was foreseen at that time was that there would be specialists on the committees, but that has not developed. We still have too much changing of Members in committees. What has been lost is the overview function which used to be provided in the House.
There is now nobody, and when 1 say "nobody" I am talking about Members of Parliament as distinct from Ministers, looking at the totality of expenditures inclusive of all government departments. In standing committees where there may be Members looking at Estimates of a particular Department, we do not find Members examining past expenditures and looking at trends. At the end of the day we come to the Public Accounts Committee which functions as an effective audit committee. However, we do not manage by audit alone. The Public Accounts Committee has the final accounting but the standing committees are not doing it at the present time.
When we consider the chain of information that is provided to Members we start with Estimates. There are Ways and Means Motions which do not necessarily always match precisely the Estimates, since there can still be Supplementary Estimates coming in to confuse matters. Then, eventually, there are the Public Accounts of Canada followed by the Auditor General's Report. Then, the Public Accounts Committee tries to establish at the end of the day that moneys were spent precisely as Parliament meant them to be spent.
I hope that since we have all-and I say "all" because it was an all-Party initiative-managed to make very substantial changes to the standing committees to achieve a higher level of functioning, Members of Parliament will come back to remember that one of the first and most important basic functions of Parliament is to control spending and ensure financial accountability. To carry this out two things are needed. First, what is needed is the will on the part of Members of Parliament, and second, clear, understandable information is needed. The quality of information provided to Members of Parliament has improved over the last 10 years, largely in response to constant pressure from the Public Accounts Committee of the House and from the recommendations of the Auditor General.
Part III of the Estimates now gives a great deal of information which provides an interested Member with the opportunity to ask questions based on financial accountability, and not only on administrative aspects of the Department.
Currency Act
If Part III of the Estimates is well used in conjunction with the Public Accounts of Canada, it can also help one to follow through the actual spending. The Auditor General has developed a further proposal; the acronym is FGRS which stands for federal government reporting study. It was a lengthy study done in co-operation with the Controller and Auditor General of the United States. I am very impressed with its potential since it gives Members a better chance to track expenditures from Estimates right through to conclusion than anything I have seen thus far.
For the busy generalist, be it Member of Parliament, journalist or interested business person, FGRS would allow one to see at a glance what has happened, whereas now one has to plough through Ways and Means Motions, Part III of the Estimates and Public Accounts. Sometimes one is frustrated in this attempt to see what has happened because different items are hidden. I am not saying that anyone has intended to hide them, but we do find apples and oranges and that measures are bulked together in a way that makes it difficult to understand.
The measure before us has to be seen in the context of attempting to provide more clear information to Members of Parliament and, of course, to the public. The next step is the commitment of Members of Parliament to use that information wisely and constantly. What is also required is a commitment from Ministers to make available this kind of information.
I was shocked to see a letter written by one of the present Ministers, admittedly one who has not had a great deal of experience in Parliament, in which, in response to a request of mine as the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee for additional information he wrote that financial control is a function of Government, not of Parliament. In this, of course, he is quite wrong. To be sure it is a responsibility of Government. It is also a responsibility of Parliament. It has been part of the basic responsibility of parliamentarians for centuries. Any Member of Parliament who forgets that is failing his or her constituents badly.
In the context of providing better information and of clarifying issues so that we know exactly what we are looking at in the Public Accounts of Canada this Bill is one additional step. It affects the presentation of the Exchange Fund account which is governed by the Currency Act. The steps that are taken by the Government today appear to be congruent with the recommendations of the Auditor General. Essentially, it repeals the three-year averaging provision. It requires the accounting principles of the Exchange Fund to conform with those used in the Public Accounts of Canada.
It is another step to make the Public Accounts of Canada more intelligible. It is a step that makes it easier for those concerned with accountability matters to find the facts that they want, and on that basis I welcome this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) for having made what, I believe, was his first speech in French in the House.

I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) on her elevation to the front bench of her Party. I notice that briefly she was occupying a front bench seat in the New Democratic Party. We welcome her here since she may not be able to get a seat in the redistribution in her own Party.
Having worked with the Hon. Member for some time I know there are few who work as hard and as consistently as she does on subjects which are difficult, complex, and not always transparent to the average elector, and her promotion is deserved.
1 wish to comment briefly on the Bill, and then perhaps a little less briefly on some of the implications related to the operations of the Exchange Fund account and the Band of Canada.
As the Minister and the critic for the Liberal Party have indicated, this is a technical Bill. It arises out of the 1986 Budget. In a modest way, it goes counter to some of the other steps that have been taken by the Government to hide its operations from average Canadians. In this particular case, it is a slightly more open accounting for the operations of the exchange fund account.
As I understand it, it appears to make a difference of between $200 million and $500 million a year in the reporting that takes place in the public accounts. It will bring the exchange fund account in line with the practices of the general public accounts. Interestingly enough, this is at a time when the banks in their operations are also moving away from smoothing and are being a little more direct on a year-to-year basis about the operations of their reserves. In a sense, this is what is happening with the Government of Canada.
If that was all there was to talk about, I could now sit down. I do wish to say a word or two, because yesterday for only the second time since his appointment we had the opportunity to have the Governor of the Bank of Canada come before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. Since the Governor is responsible for the operations of the exchange fund account, among other things, it is appropriate to take some perspective in terms of how the exchange rate for Canada is being managed or influenced by the Government and what that may mean in terms of economic policies.
I would like to express misgivings over what seems like a single-minded obsession with inflation of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, at the expense of the other objectives of economic policy. The Governor is still worried about inflation. He states that the inflation rate of approximately 4.2 per cent
is still too high. In his view, the only good rate of inflation is a zero rate of inflation. Therefore, until that goal is achieved, he does not wish to relent in terms of keeping inflation as his number one priority. He states that there can only be one monetary policy for Canada, that we cannot have any form of differential interest rates in different areas of the country. Then he states, in a rather sanguine manner, that he hopes that somehow some of the benefits of economic revival in the country might trickle down to Atlantic Canada, to the outlying parts of Quebec, and to those parts of Ontario and British Columbia which remain depressed and retain unemployment rates of 10 per cent or higher.
1 was disturbed at the manner in which the Governor of the Bank of Canada seems to tolerate what really now is a two-Canadas economic policy. We have a situation where unemployment has fallen to 2 or 3 per cent in areas such as Mississauga, west of Toronto; the unemployment rate in the industrial belt of southern Ontario and around Metropolitan Toronto is in fact down to around the 4 or 5 per cent range. I have noticed on recent visits that if people are looking for low wage service industry jobs, they are amply advertised, the want-ads are full, and one can knock on the doors of restaurants and small manufacturing establishments and probably get a job. However, a person would not be able to pay the rent because of the price of housing in the Toronto region. Nonetheless, there is employment there in a way that there was not three or four years ago.
When I say that there are two Canadas, that is demonstrated markedly when one looks at the disparities in unemployment rates between central Canada, particularly southern Ontario, and the rest of the country. Although these are the November figures, December is only a little different. The unemployment rate in Ontario is approximately 5.9 per cent. In southern Ontario it is in the order of 4.7 or 4.8 per cent. That compares with an unemployment rate of 13 per cent in Atlantic Canada, 18 per cent in Newfoundland, 13 or 14 per cent in the interior of British Columbia, 10.4 per cent in British Columbia as a whole, 10 per cent across most of the region of the Province of Quebec with the exception of Montreal, where it is a shade lower, and perhaps the area of the eastern townships.
Therefore, we have a situation where, apart from southern Ontario, unemployment rates remain at levels which are historically excessive, which are too high, and which I believe are unacceptable to average Canadians. Nonetheless, they are certainly acceptable to the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Perhaps it is easier for the bank Governor because he moves in rarefied circles, lives in comfortable housing in this, my community of Ottawa. It is a comfortable community which tends to have an economy that is not as good as but close to that of southern Ontario. The real hardship and misery of what is happening and continuing to happen in much of the country in the other Canada is simply not visible to the Governor or to his staff here in their glass tower on Wellington Street in Ottawa.
January 22, 1988

What was particularly disturbing about the evidence of the Governor was when he indicated that in his view the economy of Canada is very close to over-heating. I asked, "What would happen if the unemployment rate came down by another 1 per cent?" He said, "In that case we would be very, very close to over-heating."
We know what has happened since the crash of October 19, 1987. We know that at the time the Bank of Canada, in conjunction and in consultation with the Department of Finance, dropped interest rates sharply, injected a lot of liquidity into the economy in order to prevent a snowballing effect from the stock market crash bringing the whole economy in its wake. That has been relatively successful in the sense that we have not had a continuing and accelerating crash along the lines of what happened beginning three or four months after the great October crash of 1929. Since that time we have seen interest rates go back up both in this country and in the United States. Those rates controlled or directed by the Bank of Canada have gone up by almost a full percentage point. In other words, it has been as if that was only a little nightmare that lasted for a few weeks, but now it is over and we can go back to the real business of the Bank of Canada.
In the view of the Governor of the Bank of Canada the real business is fighting inflation. The Governor is saying that he and his bank are really there to serve as the monetary policy directors for the economy of central Canada, specifically of southern Ontario. They are now putting on the brakes because they feel that southern Ontario is about at or beyond the point of over heating.
I would suggest that that is a message of despair for people who live in Atlantic Canada with an unemployment rate of 13 per cent, and for much of Quebec with an unemployment rate of over 10 per cent. British Columbia is still reeling from the recession and it still has unemployment rates that are generally over 10 per cent. Substantial parts of the Prairies, not to mention northern Ontario, also have excessively high unemployment rates. As far as those people are concerned, they are in another Canada. They can forget about getting any kind of assistance from the Bank of Canada. They can forget about any creative and constructive use of monetary policy to try to spread the benefits of economic revival in the country to those regions. It is significant that we are now in about the fifth year of economic recovery, yet economic recovery has mainly been felt in central Canada.

That is why 1 say we now have two Canadas. We have Central Canada whose economy is concentrated in Southern Ontario around Toronto and in the Golden Horseshoe, where the unemployment rate now averages less than 5 per cent. And we have the rest of the country where the unemployment rate is still over 10 per cent, going as high as 13 per cent in the Atlantic Provinces, 18 per cent in Newfoundland, and 10 per cent or more in British Columbia.
Currency Act
When I asked the Governor of the Bank of Canada whether he was prepared to take the necessary steps to help create full employment in these regions, the answer was in fact negative, since the Governor and the Bank of Canada have a policy that is aimed at fighting inflation, despite the fact that inflation has dropped to 4.2 per cent. They see a danger of economic overheating in Ontario, which justifies maintaining interest rates at levels that are excessively high now at about 5 per cent in terms of real interest. Historically speaking, this is very high, and what this means is that they refuse to allow the economy to expand, which would benefit Quebecers and Canadians in both Eastern and Western Canada.
We have seen this particularly over the course of the time we have had the free trade negotiations. When those negotiations began the Canadian dollar was at about 72 cents. Today the dollar is just above or just below 78 cents, at a level which I believe is the highest it has been for about seven years. It is back up to that particular level.
It is interesting that the American authorities have been pressing Canada to lay off in terms of our trade surplus with the Americans and to do so by raising our exchange rates. We have done that.
It is interesting as well that the exchange fund appears to have been used in recent days specifically in order to keep the value of the Canadian dollar from going even higher and at the same time to prevent the Bank of Canada having to step in to lower Canadian interest rates. In other words, the bank is using the fund, I presume with the co-operation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and perhaps at his direction, to keep the dollar from going higher. At the same time it is adhering to its policy of interest rates which are too high because of its phobia about inflation.
My Party and I have always thought that the priorities of economic policy are not just to try to balance an adequate and acceptable level of inflation against an acceptable level of economic growth.
The third element is that full employment should be just as much an objective of government policy as is inflation control or economic growth. Because	of the	Bank of	Canada'sdirection of monetary policy	and its	influence	over the
exchange rates, I believe that the Bank of Canada must be seized with that as well. We cannot have one part of the duopoly which is governing fiscal and economic policy focusing only on inflation and leave it up to fiscal policy to do the rest in terms of trying to achieve full employment.
I was depressed when the Governor of the Bank of Canada said yesterday that there should only be one monetary policy for Canada. He did not reveal a	shade or	a smidgen	of interestin trying to find ways to work	with the	chartered banks in
order to ensure that their lending policies for real investment and real development in western Canada, Quebec, and

Atlantic Canada might in fact be more liberal or more open than their policies in southern Ontario. I do not see why that could not be done. Perhaps it cannot be done by the use of monetary instruments directly, but the Governor of the Bank of Canada, who is a man with intellectual force, and is perhaps a bit more vigorous than his predecessor, a man who is new to the job, is in a position to establish some new traditions. In fact he might well start to sit down with bank chairmen and operating officers on a regular basis to review what they are doing in order to try to get away from the structural imbalance where Ontario is close to full employment at the same time that the rest of the country is far from employment, the structural imbalance where we have two Canadas.
Monetary policy, inflation fighting, the exchange rate, and fiscal policy are all very closely intertwined. This is why I have chosen to take this opportunity to speak a bit about these interrelated questions which I think are germane, even though they extend a little beyond the narrowly defined purpose of Bill C-99. However we do not have many opportunities for this kind of discussion. It is germane as well because of what I felt were some rather wrong-headed and misdirected statements of direction by the Governor of the Bank of Canada in his testimony yesterday.
The fact as well is that many of the instruments by which government seeks to influence and change the structural problems in the economy that lead to having two Canadas will in fact be weakened because of the Government's trade deal with the United States, what I call the "American option".
The American option does not stop the Americans from using defence grants, state policies, and those kinds of things to encourage industrial development and to put jobs into regionally poor or underdeveloped areas in their country. However, the American option of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) certainly does that here in Canada. If we try to use labour market policies, training, regional development subsidies, perhaps differential rates of taxation, and fiscal policy to encourage growth in Quebec, Atlantic Canada, and British Columbia, while at the same time discourage growth in central Canada to keep the economy from overheating, we will immediately become victim to interference from the American Government and from American industries. They will shout foul and start to talk about countervailing tariffs and other types of trade actions against the output of Canadian companies. Since most Canadian companies are of a scale where they will need and in fact be encouraged to develop markets in the United States, they will be vulnerable to that, and the Government will be vulnerable to that as well.
We have a Governor of the Bank of Canada who says that he wants one monetary policy, that he cannot do anything about trying to get jobs into Newfoundland, and that in fact he will put on the brakes before Newfoundland even gets close to anything approaching full employment. At the same time we have a Conservative Government which takes an American option which effectively in the trade deal means that future governments-and I am not only talking about future
Conservative governments, but when the NDP forms a government and maybe the Liberals if they ever get to form a government again-will be constrained in using the traditional instruments of fiscal policy and the traditional tools of structural change in the economy in order to try to get a better balance among the regions of the country. I think that is very serious. In effect we are systematically stripping ourselves of the instruments and the tools that we have been using. At the same time we have the Governor of the Bank of Canada saying that he does not want to do anything about it.
I wanted to raise these particular questions. If the Governor of the Bank of Canada thinks that we are getting into an inflationary spiral before large parts of the country have even recovered from the depression, it is a very sad message indeed. One of the criteria on which the Conservative Government will be judged in the election that we expect to come this spring or this fall will be its failure to bring a lot of Canada out of the recession in which it had been plunged under the previous Liberal Government. The Government has talked about its priorities in terms of there being economic revival and national reconciliation. How the devil do you reconcile yourself to a situation if you are in Atlantic Canada where the unemployment rate is 13 per cent and the unemployment rate among young people is 18 per cent or 20 per cent? I would not reconcile myself to that. I say that is totally unacceptable.
What kind of economic revival is it, Mr. Speaker, when in Newfoundland the unemployment rate remains at 18 per cent or more? What kind of revival is that? All of that bumf has gone off to the shredder which was designed to tell people otherwise. The reason people did not take that information is that they knew it contained Tory misrepresentations of what was really going on. That, I grant you, may be a little far from Bill C-99.
I am suggesting that this area of economic policy is too little debated here in the House of Commons and should be discussed a great deal more because these questions all interrelate. It is by no accident that a governor who was obsessed with inflation has contributed to the operations of the exchange fund which has helped raise the dollar to 78 cents from 72 cents. This, in effect, has put an 8 per cent increase in costs, give or take a percentage point, on Canadian industries selling into the United States.
In other words, in order to get the deal with Washington, our monetary authorities in consultation with the Minister of Finance more or less did what they were told, which was to take some of the competitive edge off Canadian industry so that the Americans would not be so mad at us and Congress would pass the Prime Minister's American option-I have finally found the words for it that can be used in a parliamentary sense-which our Prime Minister signed.
What other deals have been made? I am not sure. I was encouraged because I think it was a sensible statement when
January 22, 1988

the Governor said that he is not wedded to a particular exchange rate for the Canadian dollar. I think that is correct. 1 think we make a bit too much over whether the dollar is at 100 cents, 78 cents or 72 cents or even at 65 cents. What is important is how Canadians are living here in this country, and not more than that. I do want to know whether there have been any secret deals made between Canada and the United States in order to encourage Congress to go ahead with this American option for Canada that will put the dollar up to 80, 82 or 84 cents sometime in the near future.
I would like some reassurance from the Government, if it has any priority for full employment, particularly in the regions, that it will reject this obsession of the Governor who is prepared to wrestle inflation to zero per cent even if it means another half a million Canadians have to go without jobs.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think when we agreed to put this Bill through today that we expected there would be some reason for which comments like the one made would be germane, but I think we can get through this within three or four minutes. Could the Minister of State for Finance comment on the recent operations of the Exchange Fund account? Specifically, will he confirm that the Government has intervened in the Exchange Fund account in order to allow the Bank of Canada to keep interest rates at their current level, a level which I think is excessive and that the Exchange Fund account is being used to control the dollar from going up as fast as it might because the Government is agreeing with the Bank of Canada that interest rates should be kept at their present level?

Mr. Chairman, I certainly cannot confirm that. I will endeavour to do some research on that for the Hon.
Currency Act
Member. I think the operation of the exchange fund account is affected by a whole host of variables. The Member mentions but one. There are many others. It would be very difficult to extract one particular determining variable and announce that that is the cause of the Exchange Fund account's differing balance at the end of each day.

Mr. Chairman, maybe 1 could pursue this a little bit and ask the Minister of State for Finance this question. Is it true that we could have prevented the dollar from rising at perhaps an excessive rate by allowing the interest rates to come down? Is it not also true-the Government talks about 120,000 jobs that might conceivably come in the 1990s from the trade deal which the Prime Minister had signed-that that reduction of interest rates would and could bring about a much bigger increase in employment and this could be done now in 1988 rather than waiting five years for the results of a trade deal which has all kinds of other adverse consequences for Canada.

speechtext: I believe the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre recognizes that fact.

We have the Governor saying that he needs to keep interest rates high because of the inflation problem. Mr. Speaker, I rise to remind the Government and particularly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) of the ongoing and unacceptable problem of aircraft noise over the Humberlea community in my riding. Mr. Speaker, as it stands, Section 30 of the Unemployment Insurance Act implicitly discriminates against the mothers of those premature babies who are most at risk and who are, for that reason, unable to come home from the hospital on their due date. Under Section 30, mothers can begin their maternity leave early should the baby arrive prior to the expected date. Alternatively, if the baby is premature and cannot leave the hospital immediately, the mother has the option of delaying her maternity leave until the expected date, at which time, presumably, the baby will be taken home from the hospital. However, there the flexibility of the Act ends. There is no provision to allow for further delays beyond the baby's expected date of arrival.
The mother of a premature baby who is not ready to come home from the hospital on her expected due date has two options. She can take her maternity leave without her baby,
January 22, 1988

which defeats the purpose of maternity leave, can prove very depressing for the mother, and in general makes little sense, or she can choose to forgo part of a leave which should be hers by right of law.
This choice is clearly unjust to a group of mothers who surely need more help rather than less, and I urge the Minister to consider changing this very important part of the Act.

CALL FOR RESIGNATION OF MINISTER OF ENERGY, MINES AND RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there appear to be two systems of justice in this country. There is one system of justice for the rich and powerful, one system for Conservative cabinet Ministers, and another system of justice for ordinary Canadians.
We have learned that a Minister of the Crown, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Masse), appears to have breached the Elections Act. It was decided that it was not in the public interest to prosecute him. I ask why is it not in the public interest to prosecute a Minister of the Crown who breaches an Act passed by this Parliament? Why is it in the public interest to prosecute ordinary Canadians who run stop signs or park illegally but it is not in the public interest to prosecute a Conservative cabinet Minister?
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) knew or ought to have known that there was sufficient evidence to prosecute and convict that Minister. He ought not to have allowed that Minister back in the Cabinet. What message does this send out to Canadians across the country? The message is very clear. If you are a Conservative cabinet Minister, there is one system of justice. If you are an ordinary Canadian, there is another system of justice.
I call on the Government of Canada to show some decency and some sense of morality and force that Minister to resign.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3, 1987, I raised in the House of Commons the case of Balkar Singh, a Canadian citizen under arrest in India, and the fact that, in the presence of both a
Canadian consular official and a doctor he made an allegation of torture.
Since that time Mr. Singh's lawyer has filed a writ of habeas corpus citing that in the presence of named senior Indian police officials he was first hamstrung from the ceiling, then someone sat between his legs and started jumping, using him as a swing. Following this, electric shocks were applied to his sexual organ, armpits and head. His legs were then forced to virtually 180 degrees. He was then beaten on the stomach and on the soles of his feet and to this day he cannot walk.
Three weeks ago a lawyer for the accused gave a copy of this sworn information to the Canadian High Commission and urgently requested a follow-up consular visit. No access has been allowed by the Indian Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prince Rupert grain handling dispute is now over and western grain farmers will breathe a sigh of relief, temporarily. As is so often the case, the Government has been called upon to intervene.

This is a law that was passed by all Parties in this House. Section 70 (3) states the following:
The Chief Electoral Office shall appoint a Commissioner of Canada Elections-whose duties, under the general supervision of the Chief Electoral Officer, shall be to ensure that the provisions of this Act are complied with and enforced.
Section 70(4) states:
No prosecution for an offence under this Act or for an offence under section 115 of the Criminal Code in relation to anything that this Act forbids or requires to be done shall be instituted except with the prior consent in writing of the Commissioner.
It is the Commissioner who has the duty, the power and the authority to press charges. In this case he exercised his judgment and discretion and chose not to do so, because of insufficient evidence, I would assume.

Where the Chief Electoral Officer has reasonable cause to believe that an

speechtext:

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: NON-SMOKING AREAS IN AIRPORT TERMINAL BUILDINGS
speechtext:
During the past four months, Transport Canada has taken several steps towards ensuring the provision of smoke-free air to those employees and passengers using airport buildings.
In late August, 1987, all airport staff were advised of the Treasury Board ban on smoking by public service employees at all service counters, waiting rooms, desks or wickets where the public is served. Employees were also advised that, as of October 1, 1987, smoking was prohibited, except for designated smoking areas, in all Public Service work places in accordance with the Treasury Board policy to phase in a total ban on smoking in all Government of Canada buildings by January 1, 1989.
Since the Treasury Board directive pertains only to government employees, Transport Canada took the initiative of issuing a directive to all its airports to restrict smoking in most areas of the air terminal buildings for the travelling public as well.

January 22, 1988
Order Paper Questions
Specifically, the directive bans smoking in all free circulation areas, ticket locations, baggage claim areas and washrooms. A minimum of 60 per cent of the seating locations in holdrooms and food and beverage outlets is designated as no smoking, and a maximum of 40 per cent of the seats in these locations can be designated as smoking. All these smoking areas are wherever possible located well away from service counters and aircraft boarding exits where passengers congregate.
In areas where there is insufficient space to properly delineate smoking and non-smoking areas, then the whole area is designated as no smoking. The only areas where smoking is freely permitted are in the bars.
To indicate smoking and no smoking areas, pictographic signs are being posted in conspicuous places inside all air terminal buildings (ATBs). Additional signs are also being posted at the main entrances of these buildings to inform the public, in both official languages, that such accommodation is provided.
Enforcement of these regulations is in accordance with the airport traffic regulations, and nay applicable municipal bylaw in cases where the airport is within the boundaries of a particular municipality.
Although public co-operation is required in order to respect the provisions outlined above, we feel that these measures will significantly improve the level of safety, comfort and health of both passengers and Transport Canada employees.

As a matter of fact, in Revenue Canada we have a joke that we do not want to be the fifty-second country, we want to be thirty-third, because we are now the thirty-third country that has gone into this harmonization of tariffs, and the United States is not one of them.
This Bill has really only to do with validating practices or decisions that were made where millions and millions of dollars of taxpayers' money was involved. The money was brought into the Treasury, and it was found in mid-1984 that perhaps the practices were not in conformity with the law, and that these instruments were signed by officials rather than by the Minister. We want to ensure that this money stays with the Canadian Treasury and get those few thousand dollars that were not received.
I would like the Bill to go through very quickly, unless the Member has something to discuss about the process. I would be delighted to answer his questions, but it has nothing to do with the agricultural aspect of this item.
Clauses 2 and 3 agreed to.
Clause 1 agreed to.

He said: Mr. Speaker, on third reading of this Bill, I would like to thank the members of both the liberal and the New Democratic Parties for their co-operation in ensuring the speedy passage of this legislation.
These amendments reduce the paper burden of corporations by bringing the reporting period under the Act in line with the fiscal period of each corporation. At the same time, these amendments give assurances that sensitive data on finances and technology transfers will remain confidential to Statistics Canada.
Equally important to these changes is the fact that the original statistical program of CALURA will be unaffected by these changes. Such reports as those that I have recently tabled will continue to shed light on aspects of foreign control and corporate concentration that are fundamental to the examination of Canadian economic issues.

subtopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to rise on Bill C-91 and indicate my Party's consent to the provisions of the Bill. We certainly agree with the necessity, where possible, to save on the reporting burden of companies, corporations, and labour unions. We agree that there is little purpose served in reporting periods that do not coincide with the fiscal period of the company or union to which the financial reporting cycle is directed.
We are glad to see the flexibility retained in the Act for the deeming powers granted the Minister in order to cope with special situations such as those where corporate mergers or reorganizations take place which may result in changes to the fiscal year. We believe that the Bill will constitute a significant measure of administrative convenience for a number of the corporations and unions, particularly the smaller ones which are reporting under the Act at present.
We are entirely in agreement with the need for Statistics Canada through the CALURA process to continue collecting information on corporate control and particularly the degree of foreign ownership within the Canadian economy. That is something that definitely has to be continued, and we are glad that there is no erosion of this objective of CALURA.
We are in broad agreement with the provision that confidential data provided by corporations should not be made too readily available to analysts within the Government. Similarly to many corporations we are concerned that they not be inadvertently granted opportunities for the use of government
Business of the House
programs to accomplish corporate data collection objectives on their competitors which, of course, are generally available through the disclosure provisions of the Securities and Exchange Commission in the United States.
The distinction between public and private corporations is one that is very germane to this Bill. We trust that the Government will continue to monitor closely any process by which public corporations are converted into private corporations, and determine the relationship between any such movement and the reporting provisions of CALURA.
I would like to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to record my Party's support of this Bill on third reading.

I have some very brief comments to make in support of Bill C-91, and on third reading I would like to say that my Party has seen fit to support this measure.
Information collected annually by the authorities will now be produced according to returns based on the fiscal instead of the calendar year. that Bill C-246, an Act to amend the Canada Elections Act (sale of liquor) be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, today it is my privilege to say a few words about this Bill, whose purpose is to remove the ban on the sale of liquor in a public place during polling hours.

1 first introduced this Bill on March 5, 1986. The House prorogued and the Bill subsequently died on the Order Paper. I reintroduced essentially the same Bill on January 26, 1987. That was almost a year ago, and here we are now finally getting a chance to address it.
A Federal Court Justice referred to this continual national frustration of the Chief Electoral Officer about a year and a half ago in the Federal Court of Canada. He said that the community should look to Parliament, not the courts, to find relief from this archaic law. This is one of the reasons I brought the matter before Parliament.
It is not new to Parliament. It has been introduced before by other Hon. Members of the House. In October 1978 the late Tom Cossitt referred to it as an archaic, Victorian anachronism and asked the House to strike out this part of the Canada Elections Act. The Hon. Member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) referred to it in May, 1982 in the same vein, as did the Hon. Member for Halton, now the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport (Mr. Jelinek). They asked the House to consider removing it from the law.
Here we go again. Finally there is a serious new twist to this archaic law, as it has been described, in that the Government of Canada in its wisdom saw fit to incorporate this particular
Private Member's Bill, word for word, into a piece of proposed government legislation, Bill C-79, which received first reading in June, 1987. Bill C-79, which I have here, incorporates word for word the two suggested sections I want to have repealed.
The prohibition can be found in Canadian legislation since shortly after Confederation. In 1970, the House amended the Canada Elections Act to restrict the prohibition to polling hours only, whereas before that 1970 date prohibition applied to the entire election day.
In the last few years some provinces have abolished the legislation within the context of provincial election campaigns. Ontario was one of them that in 1975 completely abolished the legislation at the provincial level. British Columbia did it in
1978.	Manitoba did it in 1985. Quebec now permits the sale of liquor during by-elections.
There is a certain amount of inconsistency on two counts at the national level. First, there is confusion between national and provincial responsibilities during election periods and, second, there is no prohibition at the national level during the days of advanced polling, which seems to be somewhat an anomaly as well. As we know, extensive votes are cast during advance polling hours, but anyone can have the enjoyment of imbibing if one so wishes anywhere in the country.
Confusion also exists during by-elections where an establishment on one side of the street just outside the riding within which the by-election is taking place can sell alcoholic beverages. However, an establishment inside the riding cannot do so. Obviously that confuses the public and is discriminatory in a sense.
In his last three reports following the federal elections of
1979,	1980, and 1984, the Chief Electoral Officer asked Parliament to repeal those sections of the law in order to make it clear and consistent and to bring us into the 20th century.
Some of the organizations from which I have heard recently which are very much in favour are: Red Lobster of Canada in Toronto; the Tourism Industry Association of Canada; Pacific Western Airlines, which is now part of Canadian Airlines International; the Tourism Industry Association of Alberta; Tourism Ontario Incorporated; CN Hotels; Molson Breweries; and the Ontario Motel and Hotel Association which represents 1,600 members. As we can see there is a fair amount of broad support for the proposal.
Because I have a considerable amount of faith in the process in this House, I believe that Bill C-79, which the Government introduced in June of last year, will come forth and become the new law of the land. I am not advocating any mad, passionate plea to repeal the Act. I am trying to make a rational request to bring that part of the Act into the 20th century. In the best spirit of Parliament, and so as not to use unnecessarily the resources and finances of Parliament by having the, piece of legislation I have introduced go to a legislative committee, and recognizing that the Government intends to move fairly soon to see that Bill C-79 comes back to Parliament and becomes
January 22, 1988

law before the next federal election, I seek unanimous consent of the House to have my particular Bill withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I would not want to refuse the unanimous consent for which the Hon. Member has just asked. However, perhaps we could agree informally among ourselves to proceed with the deliberations, and a few minutes before the appointed hour of adjournment, we could then proceed with giving unanimous consent. Notwithstanding the fact that the Hon. Member wants the item removed, 1 believe a number of Members would nevertheless like to speak on this very important issue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair has no objection to that. Is that suggestion agreeable to the House? The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) has asked for unanimous consent to withdraw his Bill, but one or two Members would like to say a few words. May I gather from that that after a few Members have spoken the House will give unanimous consent to the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 believe there has already been some debate on this matter, and there are a number of Members who would like to comment on the subject, but it will not take long, and we agree with the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) to have the Bill withdrawn- always, of course, with the consent of the seconder of the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Carleton (Mr. Turner) for having brought the matter to the attention of the House. As all Hon. Members will know, the present law is one that has certainly long outlived its effectiveness. We could go further and say that it has outlived its usefulness and in fact has created harm to our tourism and hospitality industries.

Prior to being in elected office I had the opportunity to work in the tourism and hospitality industry for a number of years and 1 can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that people in that industry are of the opinion that an Act of this Parliament which precludes the sale of any alcoholic beverages on the day of an election is somewhat antique in 1988. It is fine that elections are important and have to be treated seriously. Obviously any elected person in this Chamber or elsewhere is aware of that. That being said, elections are no less serious if there is a convention going on in this city where alcoholic beverages cannot be sold, which has created tremendous harm. We have within a stone's throw of this building one of the largest and most beautiful convention centres of Canada. Imagine having
1,000	delegates to a meeting there, some of whom may not even be Canadians-I am told by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton that that has happened-at the same time as a general election is taking place and the whole place
Canada Elections Act
virtually shuts down from an entertainment standpoint because of the election. I do not think that makes the electoral process any better. Frankly, 1 think it makes us look stupid and archaic.
The other proposition is one of by-elections which the Member from Ottawa-Carleton raised. If liquor were an influence on the electoral process at one time, I would suggest that in 1988 one could hardly buy someone's vote for a bottle of beer. Even if you could, the arbitrary line in the case of a by-election is what would make it legitimate to buy that bottle of beer on the north side of the street but not on the south side of the same street?
We have established, in my opinion, that this law is outdated. It is so outdated that it is nothing short of a joke. We know that around Confederation there was a period when we did not have formal ballots the way we have now. The process was far less rigorous than the one we know today. It could have been that, at the time when we were choosing people to represent us in Parliament and the process was less formal, you did not want that type of meetings totally permeated by alcoholic beverages. That does not enhance the debate in any way nor does it provide for effective representation afterwards.
At one time I suppose the availability of liquor was synono-mous or was influenced by candidates who had the wherewithal to provide it, namely, candidates with money to buy liquor for people who did not. Again, that is hardly applicable in 1988, nor do I believe that it would be meaningful in the years to come.
The law needs to be revamped. There are other sections of our election law which probably have ridiculous kinks in them as well.
To come back to the last point which the Member for Ottawa-Carleton raised in his presentation today, I would hope that our agreement as a House to withdraw this Bill later today will indicate to the Government, not that we are disinterested in the subject and, therefore, are willing to stand aside, 1 think it will be a unanimous demonstration instead of our willingness to have Bill C-79 enacted in the very near future. 1 want the Government to understand that that is at least my position. From what I see of the interest of other Members, I am sure that that would be the position of all Members of the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, I wholeheartedly support the proposal by the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) to bring this outdated and Victorian piece of legislation into the 20th century.

Just to make one point in closing on the availability of liquor in the unlikely event that someone is not convinced that the law ought to be modernized, our electoral process, as you know, has evolved into a two-tier affair, one being the nomination or the investiture by a political Party and the other one

January 22, 1988
Canada Elections Act
the election. Some nominations will have four or five thousand people attending a very large convention type of affair in order to choose a candidate. We all know that liquor is not restricted in that kind of process. While there is this two-step affair, with the first step having no restrictions at all, one could argue that in some cases there should be a little more restriction in that regard. On the other hand we have this second level, the formal electoral process. Once the candidates have been invested, the laws governing the process are, shall we say, at best useless and are at worst the laughing stock of the country. In order for any law to be effective, it should reflect the contempory view and it should have a purpose. I believe that the present Act as it pertains to liquor distribution on election day does not serve either of those two purposes and, therefore, should be altered.
Having said that, 1 want to offer my support for the initiative of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton and also my support for that portion of Bill C-79 which will modernize our Elections Act.
